title: Cross-platform SDK secret transport patterns, rotation flow, and streaming reauth ergonomics
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem statement: Our SDKs (Python/TS/Go) need a unified, secure, and ergonomic pattern for: (1) transporting credentials to the SDK runtime in hosted and private deployments, (2) performing key/token rotation without app restarts, and (3) keeping long-lived streaming connections healthy when credentials expire mid-stream. The goal of this ticket is to define concrete API ergonomics, sidecar/agent and direct-KMS patterns, retry/reauth classification, and migration guidance for existing customers.
background: Current state: various SDKs implement ad-hoc approaches: process environment variables for API keys, manual refresh callbacks for SSO tokens, or inline key refresh logic in application code. These lead to operational pain: accidental long-lived keys, brittle streaming reconnect logic, duplicated refresh implementations, and uncertain key transport semantics in private/on-prem setups. This doc proposes standardized patterns that balance security (short-lived credentials, KMS/HSM binding) with developer ergonomics (automatic refresh, clear backoff semantics, simple code paths for sync and streaming use cases).
design_decisions: Primary pattern: short-lived credentials issued by a control-plane token service (STS) with a refresh endpoint; SDKs should treat tokens as opaque, refresh via a single credential provider interface.

Sidecar pattern: for private/VPC/on-prem deployments, recommend a lightweight credential sidecar that holds long-term material (KMS/HSM or service principal) and exposes a local Unix socket/HTTP loopback to issue short-lived tokens to SDKs.
Direct KMS pattern: hosted customers may use KMS-backed signing to issue ephemeral tokens; SDKs will accept JWTs signed by customer KMS or Redwood-managed STS with audience binding.

Streaming reauth: support in-band token refresh for HTTP/2 and WebSocket streams by adding a reauth handshake frame/metadata; fallback to reconnect with resume semantics when in-band is not supported.

Retry classification: distinguish between transient network errors (retryable) and auth failures (401/403) which should trigger immediate refresh and a single retry with backoff; repeated auth failures escalate to circuit-breaker state.
Language ergonomics: provide minimal-surface credential provider interfaces per language and a streaming helper that hides refresh/reconnect details from app code.
sdk_api_guidelines: Python: provide a CredentialProvider protocol with get_token(scopes) -> Token and a StreamingSession context manager that handles reauth and reconnection transparently; prefer sync and async parity.

TypeScript: export a CredentialProvider interface returning { token: string, expiry: number } or an async getToken() promise; streaming helper should be an AsyncIterable that yields events and auto-resumes on auth refresh.

Go: define an interface TokenSource with Token(ctx) (token string, expiry time, error) and a StreamingClient that accepts a TokenSource and handles mid-stream refresh and reconnection with resume tokens.
Common: SDKs must avoid reading long-term credentials directly from process env in production; env-based bootstrap allowed only for local dev with explicit warning and short TTL default.
streaming_ergonomics: Mid-stream expiry handling: SDKs must detect server-initiated 401/402 with a special 'reauth-required' header/frame and invoke CredentialProvider to refresh and reattach credentials without losing user-visible progress when possible.

Resume tokens: for long generation streams, server should optionally return periodic resume checkpoints (opaque resume_token) that clients can provide after reconnect to continue from last checkpoint.

Backoff: after a reauth-triggered reconnect attempt, use jittered exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 10s, and cap reconnect attempts to a configurable count (default 5) before surfacing an error.
Abort signals: streaming helpers must accept an AbortController/CancelContext so caller can abort in-flight reconnect attempts.
rotation_flow: Key lifecycle: short-lived tokens (TTL 5-15m) for production SDK usage; refresh performed proactively when token lifetime remaining < 30% of TTL.
Bootstrap: SDKs may request an initial token from either (a) environment-supplied bootstrap token, (b) sidecar, or (c) metadata service (cloud-hosted).
Rotation mechanics: rotations must be atomic at the SDK provider level – swapping to new token in an atomic store to avoid races between parallel requests/streams.
Audit & key binding: tokens should include key version metadata for auditability; when using HSM/KMS, tokens should be bound to certificate thumbprint or key-id.
retry_and_error_handling: Classification: classify errors into RetryableNetwork, RateLimit, AuthFailure, ClientError. AuthFailure triggers immediate refresh attempt; network failures follow backoff policy.
Idempotency: when retrying requests after refresh, only retry idempotent operations automatically; non-idempotent streaming actions should be retried only when resume_token exists.
Circuit breaker: after N consecutive auth failures (default 3) mark provider as unhealthy and emit an SDK-level event to notify application and telemetry.
sidecar_pattern_details: Deployment: sidecar runs as a process on the host or as a Kubernetes sidecar container; exposes a local socket with mutual-TLS or file-permission restricted Unix domain socket.
API: sidecar supports endpoints: /token (issue short-lived token), /rotate (trigger manual rotation), /status, and /metrics.
Security: sidecar stores long-term credentials in encrypted form, integrates with local KMS/HSM, and provides RBAC for who can call /rotate; prefer kernel-level permissions for socket access.
Fallback: when sidecar is unreachable, SDK should fall back to configured alternate provider (env bootstrap or metadata) and log a high-severity telemetry event.
migration_plan: Phase 1: publish provider interface and sidecar spec; land SDK helpers that accept both env bootstrap and provider-based flows (beta).
Phase 2: enable short-lived tokens by default for all SDKs; ship sidecar reference implementation and deployment Helm chart for Dedicated/Private customers.
Phase 3: require token refresh behavior in major SDK vX.0 and document breaking changes; provide automated migration scripts and compatibility flag for 3 months.
Customer communication: notify customers with Dedicated/Private in two-week and one-week notices; provide migration guide and sample K8s manifests.
testing_plan: Unit tests for TokenProvider to simulate expiry, clock skew, and concurrent refresh races.
Integration tests: sidecar stub that returns deterministic tokens; simulate mid-stream reauth and checkpoint resume.
Chaos tests: network partition tests between SDK and sidecar/STS to verify fallback behavior and circuit breaker triggers.
Security tests: static analysis of credential flow, penetration test of sidecar socket permissions, and KMS integration audit checklist.
acceptance_criteria: SDKs (Python/TS/Go) expose a documented CredentialProvider abstraction and streaming helper in the next SDK release.
Reference sidecar binary and K8s Helm chart are published in infra-repo with basic docs and tests.
End-to-end integration test demonstrating a streaming session that refreshes mid-stream and resumes from a resume_token without user-visible data loss.
Security review completed and sign-off recorded on the ticket; telemetry events for auth failures and rotations are emitted.
